analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress to approve major EPA rules before they can take effect.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote in any of the six committees it was sent to, and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, an EPA rule takes effect unless Congress votes to stop it. This bill flips that: any "major" EPA rule — one costing the economy $50 million or more (down from $100 million), significantly affecting farms, or carrying a carbon price — could not take effect unless both chambers passed, and the President signed, a resolution approving it within 70 legislative days. It would also wipe out every major EPA rule already in force unless the agency resubmitted it for congressional review within 180 days.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal, oil and gas companies, large agricultural operations, and other regulated industries. Any EPA rule crossing the lowered $50 million threshold — including climate rules and rules touching farms — would face a congressional approval requirement that is very hard to satisfy in 70 legislative days, and existing major rules would be nullified unless resubmitted [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Reverses the default in the Congressional Review Act for EPA: instead of rules taking effect unless Congress disapproves, major EPA rules take effect only if Congress enacts a joint resolution of approval [S2][S3].

Lowers the 'major rule' economic threshold from $100 million to $50 million and adds new triggers: any EPA rule significantly affecting a substantial number of agricultural entities, and any rule implementing a carbon tax, counts as major [S2][S3].

Gives Congress 70 session or legislative days to approve a major rule; if no resolution is enacted in that window, the rule is deemed not approved and never takes effect, and a failed rule cannot be considered again in the same Congress [S2][S3].
Nullifies every major EPA rule in effect at enactment 180 days later unless EPA resubmits it for congressional review, and orders a GAO study tallying the total economic cost of all EPA rules [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If the bill passed, the cost would fall on people exposed to air and water pollution and to climate change: rules that curb emissions, protect air quality, or limit farm and industrial pollution could be silently vetoed by congressional inaction, since doing nothing would kill a rule just as surely as voting no [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: People exposed to pollution and climate risks

drawbacks.text: The strongest case for the bill: EPA issues billions of dollars in binding rules each year, and under the existing review law those rules take effect without Congress ever voting on them; this bill would force an explicit up-or-down decision and written cost, jobs, and related-rule disclosures for every major EPA rule [S2][S3].

As drafted, the approval requirement functions close to a blanket ban: a rule dies if Congress simply fails to act within 70 legislative days, which is the norm rather than the exception, and it could never be brought up again that Congress [S3].

The retroactive provision would nullify every existing major EPA rule after 180 days unless the agency re-ran the entire review process, creating years of legal uncertainty for states, businesses, and communities that built compliance around those rules [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A real accountability argument sits behind the bill — Congress writes environmental laws but rarely votes on the rules that fill them in. But the mechanism is so demanding that its practical effect would be the quiet elimination of most major EPA rulemaking, plus the retroactive erasure of rules already in force. The public cost in forgone air, water, and climate protections would far outweigh the procedural benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to six House committees and then three subcommittees, no committee ever reported it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Sam Graves introduced the bill on July 9, 2014, and the Speaker referred it to six committees: Judiciary, Energy and Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, Agriculture, Rules, and Budget [S1][S5].
Within days it was further referred to subcommittees on Water Resources and Environment, Environment and the Economy, and Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law [S5].
No committee or subcommittee reported the bill, no resolution was ever taken up, and no vote occurred in either chamber before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, EPA's major rules — including the climate and air quality rules then in the pipeline — kept their normal path into effect, and the industries that would have gained a congressional veto over them got nothing. Existing environmental protections stayed on the books.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: EPA rules and the public they protect

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never advanced far enough to produce a floor vote.

industries.note: In 2014 the EPA was writing carbon and air-quality rules affecting coal; the bill would have let congressional inaction kill any such rule costing $50 million or more, and would have nullified existing major rules. That shields the industry's compliance costs at the expense of air quality for people living downwind [S1][S2][S3].
Any EPA rule touching carbon pricing or emissions from oil and gas combustion would require explicit congressional approval to take effect, making new safeguards far easier to block [S3].

The bill adds a new trigger making any EPA rule with a significant impact on a substantial number of agricultural entities a 'major rule' subject to congressional approval, giving farm interests a procedural veto over pollution rules that affect them [S2][S3].
Lowering the major-rule threshold to $50 million doubles the number of EPA rules needing congressional sign-off, delaying or killing rules these industries bear compliance costs under [S2].
